en: Now, besides the levels of abstraction and
the different kinds of operations you might
be doing in a function,
there is another reason for why you might
wanna split a function into smaller pieces.
And that would be reusability because
reusability matters, at least sometimes.
In programming, whenever you write any code,
there is one very important rule. Which you
should try to follow as often as possible.
In the best case, of course, you should
always follow it. And that rule is that you
shouldn't repeat yourself.
Don't repeat yourself, write DRY code.
That's something you will hear a lot and DRY
code simply means code where you don't
repeat yourself.
And this is not a complex concept at all. It
simply means
don't write the same code or very similar
code in more than one place
because if you do, you are repeating
yourself. And what's the problem with
repeating yourself?
Well, whenever you need to change something
about that code, some logic or some error,
then you need to make this change in
multiple places throughout your application
if you did repeat yourself.
If you never repeated yourself, then you
only need to make the change once, which is
of course way better.
Now, here are some signs for code which is
not DRY, so where you are repeating
yourself.
One obvious sign, of course, is that you
find yourself copy and pasting code. If
you're doing that, you are obviously
repeating yourself.
But another sign would be that you do need
to change something and you see that you
need to apply basically the same change in
different places in your codebase?
Well, the reason for that probably is that
you did repeat yourself.
